Gathers.lead: Gathering draws fabric together at selected points, creating folds that open into fullness. The garments and artworks presented here invite us to examine how these folds both reveal and shape the body beneath.
paragraphs: Where do you notice gathers on the pieces in this case? Perhaps you see them falling from a neckline, crossing the torso in diagonals, or emerging at the waistline before opening into a full skirt. These arrangements create volume and alter the body’s proportions. Long vertical folds make a figure appear taller, while those drawn across the torso direct attention to its curves.

Follow the folds with your eyes. Where do they begin, which way do they travel, and where are they released? Look at the garments and artworks to compare how fabric takes shape and creates shape. How do these different arrangements suggest and sculpt the body beneath the cloth?

Pleats.lead: Pleats are clearly defined folds in fabric, which are typically linear in nature and consist of exterior folds and interior folds.
paragraphs: There are many ways to create pleat structures. For instance, the exterior folds of a knife pleat all point in the same direction and are created through overlapping, whereas a box pleat sets knife pleats back-to-back so that the exterior edges “kiss” (they are sometimes referred to as kissing pleats for this reason). Accordion pleats alternate back-and-forth in a zigzag. The sunburst pleat begins narrow at the top and increases its width down the length of the fabric to add greater fullness. When a pleat is rounded rather than sharp at its edge, it is referred to as fluting. The shape and scale of a pleat’s peaks and hollows catch light differently, creating variations in light and shadow across the garment’s surface.

The repetition of pleating creates a sense of rhythm as our eyes follow one line after another across the garment. The direction, size, and shape of these lines change how we see the body. Vertical lines lead the eye along the body, while diagonal or curving lines carry it across and around the figure. Pleats expand and contract in response to the body’s curves, sometimes softening them into a column-like silhouette, and other times expanding them to create volume.

Across this case, pleats take shape in both natural silks and synthetic fabrics. Polyester can be heat-set to ensure the permanence of the pleats, whereas silk and other natural materials will lose shape over time in response to the body living within the garment. The fiber type and weight of the fabric will affect how folds fall, hold their shape, and respond to movement. Fabric moves with the body wearing it, causing the pleat lines to spread, gather, and change. How might patterns of light and shadow change as the wearer walks, dances, and extends their arms?

Layers.lead: Layering places one fabric over another, building multiple outlines around the body. An outer layer might wrap across the chest, hang from the shoulders, or fall behind the wearer’s back. Its shape depends on where it is held and how freely it hangs.
paragraphs: Layers change how much of the body we see and how we imagine the parts they hide. Loose folds conceal parts of the figure, while openings and sheer fabric reveal others. Through a transparent layer, the outline beneath remains visible, allowing us to see two shapes at once. Cloth can enclose the figure while still allowing its shape to be visible.

The space between cloth and body becomes part of the garment’s shape, changing how we see the wearer beneath it. Compare the garments with the three terracotta figures on the pedestal. How do their layers suggest the body beneath them? Where does each layer follow the body, and where does it create a shape of its own?

Posture.lead: Posture describes the body’s position in space. Comportment refers to the way a body is held and how we carry ourselves, which reflects culturally specific learned ways of standing and moving. Ancient Greek sculptors used contrapposto to make standing figures appear more lifelike. In this position, one leg carries most of the body’s weight, while the hips and shoulders tilt in different directions, creating an asymmetrical balance.
paragraphs: Clothing can reflect a similar kind of balance without changing the body’s pose. An angled neckline can draw the eye toward one shoulder, while folds that cross the waist lead it toward the opposite hip. Contrast between sheer and solid fabric gives some areas more visual weight, which draws the eye and creates emphasis.

These details influence how we read a figure: do they appear relaxed, restrained, or ready to move? Compare the shoulders, waist, and hips: does the clothing reinforce the figure’s stance or suggest a different one? What impressions of the wearer emerge?

Ancient World: Greece.lead: This case takes ancient Greek ornament as a starting point for exploring decorative traditions across the Mediterranean. A motif is a decorative shape or image that can be repeated to form a pattern. On textiles, these designs can be printed, woven, embroidered, or formed with beads, sequins, stones, and other attachments. Displayed alongside Greek ceramics, the garments invite us to consider how ornament directs attention and organizes a surface.
paragraphs: The placement of ornament matters as much as the motif itself. Borders emphasize edges, decorated necklines frame the face, and bands around the waist divide a garment into sections. Repeated motifs establish a visual rhythm, while clustered decoration draws the eye to a particular area. Contrasts between plain cloth and densely patterned areas heighten these effects.

Compare a border around a ceramic vessel with one along a neckline or hem. What leads your eye across the surface, and where does it pause? Similar arrangements can connect these objects visually, but their motifs may carry different meanings within particular historical and cultural contexts.

Ancient World: Egypt.lead: In ancient Egypt, gold’s color and radiance linked it to the sun and the gods. Centuries later, fascination with ancient Egypt—often called Egyptomania—inspired art, architecture, and fashion. The discovery of Tutankhamun’s tomb in 1922 renewed this interest, bringing images of its rich colors and golden treasures to a wide audience.
paragraphs: Designers used beads, metal, and reflective threads to evoke their own visions of ancient Egypt’s splendor. The visual impact of these materials depends partly on contrast: bright ornament stands out against dark cloth, making a border or pattern more distinct.

Texture also shapes how a surface reflects light, which in turn affects perception of color. Smooth materials can produce broad flashes, while beads and textured threads create smaller, scattered highlights. As the wearer moves, these reflections shift and change which details stand out. Compare the garments: where does reflected light shimmer and shine to emphasize a pattern, and where does color alone draw your eye?
